name: Ben Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the office for a climate charity, about thirty staff, half of them remote. My mornings are the shared calendar, room bookings, supplier invoices and the volunteer rota. I've built a bunch of little AI helpers that sort the inbox and draft the weekly bulletin, so my afternoons go on the bits that need a person. I like making the place run so smoothly that nobody notices.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Grant reporting season. Every funder wants the same numbers in a different template, and I end up up late reformatting spreadsheets. I've started using AI to do the first pass, which has saved me about a day a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly, because I'd hoped the tools would get better. I'd post something like: fine, it's a good spellchecker with ambitions. At work I'd say we keep using what helps and drop what doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine in that world. I'm already ahead on the tools, the charity values me, and the jobs I'd go for nearby would still exist. The real pressure is funding, because charity money goes up and down with the economy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my little automations running and maybe teach the other two admins to build their own. I'd keep saving about a fifth of my pay, which gives me roughly four months now. I'd also start a free course on data reporting so I'm better at the grant stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. I like change, so a world where nothing happens is a bit boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned funding. How exposed is the charity?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We lost a big foundation grant two years ago and had to let two campaigners go. Admin's usually the last thing cut because someone has to keep the lights on. But I keep an eye on the reserves report every quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Jo fixes bikes, and Jo says nobody's automating a seized chain. The workshop's a co-op down the road, and Jo laughs at all my AI stuff. We'd joke about it over dinner, but the bike shop is busier than ever.

say: I'd joke that AI is a **good spellchecker** with ambitions.
At work I'd say keep what **helps** and drop what doesn't.
think: I'm **ahead on the tools** and valued, so I'm secure here.
The real pressure is **charity funding**, which rises and falls with the economy.
do: Keep his **automations** running and teach two colleagues to build their own.
Keep saving about **a fifth** of his pay.
Start a free **data reporting** course to improve grant work.
S0.quote: My partner Jo fixes bikes, and Jo says nobody's automating a seized chain.
fieldNote: He's the rare person **disappointed** by the plateau.
His risk is **funding**, not technology, and he tracks reserves himself.
His partner's **hands-on** job is a running joke that later becomes serious.

steps.text: Teach the two other admins to build simple inbox automations
Keep saving about a fifth of each month's pay
Take a free online course in data reporting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure workers get a say in how the tools are used. I'd be posting about shorter hours, not fewer jobs. At work I'd volunteer to lead the rollout, because better me than a consultant who doesn't know us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my own role probably grows, because someone has to set the tools up and check them. But the other two admins, Priya and Tom, are exactly the jobs that shrink. That bothers me more than my own position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write a plan for the charity's director within a month, saying which tasks we automate and how Priya and Tom move into volunteer coordination and events. I'd book myself onto a proper course on workflow automation. And I'd join the union the charity sector has, which I've been meaning to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for other people. I'm a bit excited too, which feels awkward to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the director just wants to cut Priya and Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd argue hard, and I'd have the numbers ready to show the money saved could pay for their new roles. If she still said no, I'd be in a really uncomfortable place. I'd probably stay, but I wouldn't feel good about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're excited. About what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About finally not reformatting funder spreadsheets at midnight. If the boring stuff goes, I get to do the bits I'm actually good at, like sorting problems and looking after people. I just want that to be true for everyone, not only me.

say: I'd say workers need a **say** in how the tools are used.
I'd post about **shorter hours**, not fewer jobs, and volunteer to lead the rollout.
think: My role probably **grows**, because someone has to set up and check the tools.
Colleagues Priya and Tom hold **exactly the jobs** that shrink.
do: Write the director a **plan** within a month to move Priya and Tom into events.
Book a proper course on **workflow automation**.
feel: **Uneasy** for his colleagues, and a little **excited**, which he feels awkward about.
S1.quote: If the boring stuff goes, I get to do the bits I'm actually good at, like sorting problems and looking after people.
fieldNote: He expects to **gain** while colleagues lose, and feels the tension.
His instinct is to **lead the change** from inside rather than resist it.
His politics show in a concrete **redeployment plan**, not just slogans.

steps.text: Lead the charity's rollout of the new admin software
Write the director a plan to move Priya and Tom into events
Take a course on workflow automation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this needs a universal basic income, now, not in a white paper in five years. I'd be online every day pushing for it. At work I'd say we should use the two years to protect people, not just cut costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone too, maybe a year after the others. If AI can do any thinking work, it can set up its own workflows. Being good with the AI tools buys me months, not years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use those months well. I'd ask Jo about learning bike repair properly at the co-op, because hands-on work has until about 2031. I'd up my savings to a third of my pay and stop the holiday fund. And I'd join every campaign for basic income going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but strangely energised. I'd rather act than sit with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So you'd follow Jo into bike repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, or something like it, fixing heat pumps or solar panels, which fits the climate stuff I care about. I'd have three years before robots catch up there, which is a long time if you start the week AGI lands. It's not forever, but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the charity itself closes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd probably get a few months' redundancy pay, and Jo's income would carry the rent for a bit. We'd be tight, but we'd be okay for half a year. After that I'd need the new trade to be paying.

say: I'd push for a **universal basic income** now, not in five years.
At work I'd say use the **two years** to protect people, not cut costs.
think: My job goes too, maybe **a year later** than the others.
Being good with tools buys me **months**, not years.
do: Start learning **bike or heat pump** repair, since robots lag thinking AI by three years.
Raise savings to **a third** of his pay and drop the holiday fund.
feel: **Anxious** but **energised**, preferring action to sitting with it.
S2.quote: Being good with the AI tools buys me months, not years.
fieldNote: He sees through the idea that **early adopters** are safe from AGI.
His move to **hands-on climate work** joins his values with the robot gap.
Jo's **income** is the household's backstop, which steadies him.

steps.text: Learn bike repair at Jo's co-op or train in heat pump fitting
Raise savings to a third of his pay
Campaign online and in person for basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if we start now, and I'd push hard for that at the charity and online. I'd say the climate sector needs hands-on workers anyway, so let's retrain office people into that. I'd probably give a talk at our team day about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel okay. My office job still goes, but I'd have time to train in heat pump fitting properly and be qualified before the AI even arrives. That's a good position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a heat pump installer course in the first year, evenings and weekends. I'd keep managing the office and keep automating it, because that's the job until it isn't. I'd save a quarter of my pay towards the gap between careers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a lot of hope mixed in. Five years of warning feels like a door rather than a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd automate your own office while planning to leave. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honest, actually. I'd tell the director what I'm doing and why. It's better than pretending the job will last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Priya and Tom in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to bring them with me, at least tell them about the courses. Tom's handy, he'd be good at installs. Priya's more of a people person, so maybe care work or teaching.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to plan if we start now.
I'd argue the climate sector should **retrain office staff** into hands-on work.
think: My office job still goes, but I can **qualify** before AGI arrives.
Heat pump fitting gives me a **good position** with time to spare.
do: Sign up for an evening **heat pump installer** course in the first year.
Keep **automating** the office while still managing it.
Save **a quarter** of his pay for the gap between careers.
feel: **Uneasy** but **hopeful**, seeing it as a door rather than a wall.
S3.quote: Five years of warning feels like a door rather than a wall.
fieldNote: He's open with his director about **planning to leave**.
He wants to bring **colleagues** with him, matching his politics.
Five years of warning gives his plan a **realistic timetable**.

steps.text: Enrol on an evening heat pump installer course
Keep automating the charity's office tasks
Save a quarter of his pay for the career gap

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty if we're serious, and I'd be pushing government to fund green trades training on a big scale. I'd say it at work and online, often. I'd be the optimist in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'd have years to try things, and the office job would probably grow before it shrinks, because someone has to run the tools. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI lands, with a trade and an office background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the office and get much deeper into automation, maybe even help other small charities set up their systems on the side. I'd start the heat pump course within two years, not rushing it. I'd keep saving a fifth and might talk to Jo about buying a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Helping other charities on the side, would you charge for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a small day rate, maybe one Saturday a month. It'd bring in a bit of extra money for the deposit. It'd also teach me how other places run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people will waste it. Ten years sounds long, so governments do nothing for eight and panic for two. I'd want people like me pushing the whole time.

I'd say a decade is **plenty** if we're serious.
think: The office job would **grow before it shrinks** because someone runs the tools.

fieldNote: His one worry here is **political**: that the time gets wasted.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time for anyone to bring their colleagues along. What would help is a basic income, so people can retrain without losing their homes. And free trades courses that don't have two-year waiting lists.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people would do if money wasn't the problem. I think a lot of office people would happily fix things, plant trees or look after old folk. We've just never been paid enough to try.

headlineQuote: A lot of office people would happily fix things, plant trees or look after old folk.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old** office manager at a climate charity who builds his own **AI helpers**.
He's **progressive**, pushes for **basic income**, and worries more for colleagues than himself.
He's **adaptive** and would retrain into **heat pump** fitting, using the robot delay.
He's **calm** in AI Plateau and AGI by 2036, but **anxious** when AGI comes in two years.
His partner **Jo** fixes bikes and carries the household if his job goes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to bring **colleagues** along.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** while people retrain, and free **trades courses** without long waiting lists.
